new_statements.quote: However, such a restriction might be a consequence of a more general constraint stipulating that no content word has an stressed open syllable with a short vowel. Thus, it seems that the occurrence of Falling tone depends, at least partially, on prosodic conditions, such that only the syllable of a word with primary stress is able to bear the contour. [p. 166] // Some data suggest that the the permissible weight of the nucleus in the stressed syllable of content words (particularly, those in root and stems) is two moras. [p. 132]
new_statements.citation: Avelino Becerra, Heriberto. 2004. Topics in Yalálag Zapotec, with particular reference to its phonetic structures. PhD dissertation, University of California, Los Angeles.
new_statements.locator: sec. 4.5.2 'YZ Tone and the Typology of Contour Tone Restrictions', p. 166 (PDF page 189); supporting passage sec. 4.4.1, p. 132 (PDF page 155)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yalálag Zapotec is a tone language (High, Low, Falling). Avelino gives no explicit stress-placement rule; his statements presuppose one stressed (primary-stress) syllable per content word, which is the root/stem syllable: roots are typically monosyllabic, the stressed nucleus is bimoraic (long vowel, diphthong, or vowel plus coda), and only the primary-stressed syllable can carry Falling tone. Bisyllabic Spanish loans are transcribed with stress on the syllable that was stressed in Spanish (e.g. ka'ba3, ku'pad, pan'dank, sep'tjembr, p. 154), which ends up as the word-final/stem syllable. Provisionally: stress is morphologically fixed on the (usually monosyllabic) root/stem syllable, not on affixes or clitics; a positional label cannot be assigned from this source.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only one remark: the infinitive prefix w- before vowel-initial stems is 'a very short gesture, without independent (secondary) stress' and is not parsed as a separate syllable (p. 144).
new_statements.exceptions: Loan word par'jid < Spanish pálido is called 'still problematic' because Spanish stress is initial but the YZ form keeps the final syllable (p. 156). No native-word exceptions discussed.
new_statements.domain_note: Statements concern content words/roots and stems (lexical word level) and loanword adaptation; no discussion of phrase-level accent. Tone, not stress, is the contrastive prosody; stress is treated as a prosodic condition on tone-bearing and syllable weight.
new_statements.identity_note: Avelino 2004 describes the Zapotec of Villa Hidalgo Yalálag itself (speakers recorded in Yalálag and in the Los Angeles diaspora), i.e. yala1267/zpu proper. Hernández Andrade 2011 describes two varieties spoken in San Juan Jaltepec (Choapan district), one of Yalálag origin and one of Santa María Yahuivé/Choapan origin (zpc); it contains no stress statement.

sources.note: No dedicated stress section; stress is mentioned incidentally: content words (roots/stems) have a stressed syllable whose nucleus is bimoraic (p. 132); no content word has a stressed open syllable with a short vowel, and only the syllable with primary stress can bear Falling tone (p. 166); YZ prefers monosyllabic roots and to some extent monosyllabic words (p. 152), Spanish loans keep the Spanish stressed syllable as the locus of the borrowing and are adapted preferably as monosyllables (pp. 153-156); infinitive prefix w- has no independent (secondary) stress (p. 144); Newberg 1983 is reporte…

sources.note: No statement on word stress; 'acento' occurs only as the written tone mark ('los tonos altos... se marcan con acento', p. 12). Describes tones (level high/low, contour rising/falling) and consonant/vowel inventories of two Zapotec varieties in San Juan Jaltepec (one of Yalálag origin) and cites Avelino 2004 for Yalálag.
